name: Classical-Middle Armenian
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.

new_statements.quote: § 37 — Seitdem in vorhistorischer Zeit sich ein kräftiger Stärkeakzent auf der vorletzten Silbe des Wortes festgesetzt hatte und in Auswirkung davon — aber erst nach der Aufnahme der zahlreichen mittelpersischen (arsakidischen) Lehnwörter — die letzte Wortsilbe infolge Schwachtonigkeit geschwunden war, herrschte im Altarmenischen so gut wie ausschließlich die Ultimabetonung, eine Betonung, die im modernen Westarmenisch sowie in der ostarmenischen Literatursprache noch heute befolgt wird. Dabei ist es gleichgültig, ob die nunmehr letzte Silbe eine Stamm- oder Endungssilbe ist; z. B. t‘agawór „König”, gen. t‘agawori, t‘agaworakan „königlich”, t‘agaworec‘uc‘anel „zum König krönen”. Wenn nach § 24 am Wortende zwischen zwei Konsonanten ein ə gesprochen wird, so zieht dieses nicht den Akzent auf sich, also akn „Auge”, gespr. ákən.
new_statements.translation: § 37 — Since in prehistoric times a strong stress accent had settled on the penultimate syllable of the word and, as a consequence of this — but only after the borrowing of the numerous Middle Persian (Arsacid) loanwords — the final syllable of the word had been lost through weak stress, ultima stress prevailed in Old Armenian almost without exception, a stress placement which is still followed today in modern Western Armenian as well as in the Eastern Armenian literary language. It makes no difference whether the now-final syllable is a stem syllable or an ending syllable; e.g. t‘agawór 'king', gen. t‘agaworí, t‘agaworakán 'royal', t‘agaworec‘uc‘anél 'to crown as king'. When, according to § 24, a ə is pronounced at the end of the word between two consonants, it does not attract the accent; thus akn 'eye', pronounced ákən.
new_statements.citation: Jensen, Hans. 1959. Altarmenische Grammatik. Heidelberg: Carl Winter.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record's final-stress rule (final stress) and adds the epenthetic-schwa provision, the historical penult-to-ultima account, the clitic behaviour, the vowel-reduction consequences, and the closed list of first-syllable-stressed univerbations/interjections (with -ik words stressed on the second syllable).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the last syllable of the word, regardless of whether that syllable belongs to the stem or to an inflectional/derivational ending; an epenthetic schwa pronounced between two word-final consonants does not count and does not take the stress. Jensen frames this as the outcome of a prehistoric penultimate stress after which the original final syllable was apocopated. The strong stress causes reduction of i, u (syncope or schwa), ē > i, oy > u, ea > e when a syllable becomes non-final and hence unstressed (§ 38).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Proclitics (prepositions, postpositions, conjunctions, the negation oč‘ > č‘-) carry no stress of their own within the sentence; the copula forms (em, es, etc.) are enclitic to the preceding stressed word.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Ausnahmen von der dargestellten Betonung sind im Grunde nur scheinbar' (p. 19): apparent exceptions are univerbations (Zusammenrückungen) of pronouns and words like 'measure, manner' where emphasis puts the tone on the first element, e.g. aysp‘ēs 'so', aysč‘ap‘ 'so much', orč‘ap‘ 'how much', orp‘ēs 'how', ahawasik / ahawadik 'voici, voilà', grēt‘ē 'almost', mananawand 'especially', the interjections p‘u and hapa; in these the accent lies on the first syllable, except those ending in -ik which stress the second syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Jensen describes Classical Armenian (Altarmenisch, grabar, the language of the 5th-century texts); he adds that the same final stress holds in modern Western Armenian and in the Eastern Armenian literary language, and remarks (§ 44 Anm.) that the syncope in the singular forms of Astuac 'God' is Middle Armenian rather than Classical. The catalog item clas1249 'Classical-Middle Armenian' covers this variety.

tone_statements.citation: Olsen, Birgit Anette & Rasmus Thorsø. 2022. Armenian. In Thomas Olander (ed.), The Indo-European Language Family: A Phylogenetic Perspective, ch. 12, 202-222. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
tone_statements.quote: 5. Loss of tonal accent and fixation of stress, at first on the penultimate syllable, eventually leading to syncope of all final syllables. With few exceptions, stress is thus synchronically fixed on the final syllable. 6. At a later stage than (5), weakening of unstressed high vowels and diphthongs, whereby i and u become [ə] (usually unwritten), ē becomes i, oy becomes u, while ea becomes e.
tone_statements.locator: ch. 12 'Armenian', sec. 12.2.1 'Phonological Innovations', subsection 'Vowels and Semivowels', items 5-6 (pp. 202-222; exact page not visible in the HTML edition)
tone_statements.summary: No tone: the inherited tonal (pitch) accent was lost and replaced by a stress accent, fixed on the final syllable in Classical Armenian.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, final syllable: final stress) rests on Meillet 1913 sec. 23, which I downloaded from the cited archive.org item and confirmed verbatim at p. 16. Three further open sources downloaded now agree: Thomson 1989 p. 14-15 ('always stressed on the last full syllabic', epenthetic schwa before final nasal/liquid not counted), Meillet 1903 Esquisse sec. 5 (final accent from the start of the historical period, persisting into medieval Cilician and most modern dialects), and Karst 1901 (Cilician/Middle Armenian, presupposes final = stressed). The only nuances (proclitic/enclitic unstressed words; a few adverbs/compounds like orpēs analysed by Meillet as word groups; epenthetic ə not counted) do not affect a fixed: final syllable classification and could populate the empty 'domain'/'edge' fields ('last full vowel; epenthetic ə excluded'). sources.citation: DeLisi, Jessica L. 2015. Epenthesis and prosodic structure in Armenian: A diachronic account. PhD dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles (Indo-European Studies). xvi+127 pp. (eScholarship item 3mk6z9mq)
sources.note: States that the PIE mobile pitch accent system left few if any traces in Armenian and 'must simply have been entirely given up' in Proto-Armenian, all Armenian varieties having a stress-based accent; Classical Armenian has persistent final-syllable primary stress (orthographic evidence: accent marks and question-mark placement in Gospel ms. E, Kuenzle 1984; phonological evidence: high-vowel/diphthong reduction under stress shift); discusses possible initial secondary stress (hammock pattern) reconstructed for Proto-Armenian. No lexical or grammatical tone.

tone.quote: The prosodic system traditionally reconstructed for Proto-Indo-European has left few, if any, traces on the Armenian language. ... Classical Armenian texts exhibit both orthographic and phonological evidence for persistent stress on the final syllable of the word. ... Since all Armenian varieties show a persistent stress-based accent on the final or penult syllable of the word and most attest to secondary stress on the initial syllable, the Proto-Indo-European system must simply have been entirely given up at some point in the Proto-Armenian period.

tone.summary: No tone: the inherited PIE pitch accent was abandoned; Classical Armenian has a stress accent fixed on the final (full) syllable, with a few initially-accented adverbs/interjections and possibly initial secondary stress.
